records.source: Καυχᾶσθαι δεῖ· οὐ συμφέρον μέν, ἐλεύσομαι δὲ εἰς ὀπτασίας καὶ ἀποκαλύψεις κυρίου.
records.gloss: To boast it is necessary; not profitable indeed, I will come but to visions and revelations of [the] Lord.
pieces: I have to boast. It does no good, but now I will turn to visions and revelations given by the Lord.

L.1: It is necessary to boast; it is not profitable, but I will go on to visions and revelations of [the] Lord.

R.1: I must go on boasting. It does not do any good, but I will do it. Now I will tell about visions and things the Lord has shown me.

decisions.choice: it is necessary to boast: Paul is pushed into boasting by the situation in Corinth
alternatives: boasting is a duty in itself
decisions.reason: Καυχᾶσθαι δεῖ ("to boast is necessary") picks up the boasting Paul began in 11:16-33, the "fool's speech" he takes up against his rivals. The necessity is not a rule but the pressure of the moment: in 12:11 he says the Corinthians forced him to it, because they did not speak up for him.

decisions.choice: not profitable: boasting does no real good
decisions.reason: οὐ συμφέρον means "not beneficial, not useful". Paul grants that boasting builds no one up (compare 12:19, where all he does is for their building up), yet he goes on because the situation demands it.

decisions.choice: visions and revelations from the Lord: given by the Lord
alternatives: visions and revelations in which the Lord is seen
decisions.reason: The genitive κυρίου ("of [the] Lord") most naturally names the giver: the Lord granted these experiences. It could also include the Lord as what was seen, and the two senses overlap. "Lord" here is most likely Christ, as in 12:8-9.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "it is necessary to boast; it is not profitable, but I will go on"
alternatives: later manuscripts: "boasting is not profitable for me, for I will go on"
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ in the first words of the verse: many later manuscripts read a particle instead of δεῖ, add "for me" and join the clauses differently, which is the reading of the King James Version. The meaning is close either way. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: boast (L, B, R)
decisions.reason: In 2 Corinthians 10-12 Paul's argument turns on the word itself, so all three levels keep "boast" here and through the chapter, as the book-wide choice for these chapters settles.

decisions.choice: Now I will tell about visions and things the Lord has shown me
alternatives: I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable explains "revelations" as things the Lord has shown and says that Paul is moving to a new subject.

records.heading: Visions and a thorn in the flesh

records.source: οἶδα ἄνθρωπον ἐν Χριστῷ πρὸ ἐτῶν δεκατεσσάρων εἴτε ἐν σώματι οὐκ οἶδα, εἴτε ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος οὐκ οἶδα, ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν ἁρπαγέντα τὸν τοιοῦτον ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ.
records.gloss: I know a man in Christ before years fourteen, whether in [the] body not I know, or outside of the body not I know, the God knows, having been caught up the such [one] up to [the] third heaven.
pieces: Fourteen years ago a man I know, a man in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, was snatched away as far as the third heaven. Whether this happened in the body or outside the body, I do not know. God knows.

L.2: I know a man in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, fourteen years ago (whether in [the] body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows), such a [man] caught up as far as [the] third heaven.

R.2: I know a man who belongs to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. Fourteen years ago he was taken up into the third heaven. I do not know if he was in his body or out of his body when it happened. Only God knows.

decisions.choice: a man in Christ: Paul is speaking of himself in the third person
decisions.reason: Verse 7 shows that the man is Paul: the revelations were so great that he himself was given a thorn to keep him humble. He speaks of "a man" to keep the experience at a distance, as something given to him and not an achievement he can take credit for (verse 5). ἄνθρωπον here is one particular man, not people in general. "In Christ" means a believer, one who belongs to Christ.

decisions.choice: fourteen years ago: counted back from the time of writing
decisions.reason: πρὸ ἐτῶν δεκατεσσάρων counts back from when Paul writes. If 2 Corinthians was written in the mid-50s, the experience falls in the early 40s, years before Paul came to Corinth. The Corinthians had evidently never heard of it, which shows how little Paul made of it.

decisions.choice: the third heaven: the highest heaven, where God is
alternatives: one of seven heavens, not the highest
decisions.reason: Jewish writings of the time could speak of several heavens, above the sky and the stars. Here "the third heaven" is the highest one, the place of God's presence, and verse 4 calls the same place paradise. Some Jewish texts count seven heavens, but nothing in the passage suggests Paul means a lower level.

decisions.choice: caught up: suddenly seized and carried away by God's power
decisions.reason: ἁρπαγέντα is a passive of the verb for snatching or seizing. The same verb is used for believers being caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17) and for Philip being carried away by the Spirit (Acts 8:39). Paul did not ascend by his own effort; he was taken.

decisions.choice: whether in the body or outside the body: Paul does not know how it happened
alternatives: Paul denies that the body was involved
decisions.reason: The repeated οὐκ οἶδα ("I do not know") and ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν ("God knows") interrupt the sentence. Paul is sure of the experience but not of its manner, whether he was taken bodily or only in spirit, and he leaves that to God.

decisions.choice: a man, with no gender setting
decisions.reason: The word refers to one particular man, Paul himself (m1), so it takes no gender setting.

decisions.choice: Fourteen years ago a man I know ... was snatched away as far as the third heaven. Whether this happened ...
alternatives: keeping the interruption in the middle of the sentence
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the main statement first and the interruption about the body after it, so that the sentence can be followed when read aloud.

records.source: καὶ οἶδα τὸν τοιοῦτον ἄνθρωπον εἴτε ἐν σώματι εἴτε χωρὶς τοῦ σώματος οὐκ οἶδα, ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν ὅτι ἡρπάγη εἰς τὸν παράδεισον καὶ ἤκουσεν ἄρρητα ῥήματα ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι.
records.gloss: And I know the such man, whether in [the] body or apart from the body not I know, the God knows, \v 4 that he was caught up into the paradise and heard unspeakable words which not being permitted for a man to speak.
pieces: This same man, I know (in the body or apart from it, I do not know; God knows),
was snatched away into paradise. There he heard things beyond speaking, which no human being is allowed to tell.

L.3: And I know such a man (whether in [the] body or apart from the body I do not know; God knows),
L.4: that he was caught up into paradise and heard unutterable words, which a human being is not allowed to speak.

R.3: I also know this about that man. I do not know if he was in his body or out of it; God knows.
R.4: But I know that he was taken up into paradise. There he heard things too holy to put into words, things no person is allowed to repeat.

decisions.choice: the same experience told a second time
decisions.reason: Verses 3-4 repeat the wording of verse 2 almost exactly, with the same interruption about the body. The repetition is solemn emphasis, and "paradise" names the same place as "the third heaven". Some have read two stages of one journey, but nothing in the text marks a second event.

decisions.choice: paradise: the place of God's presence and blessing
alternatives: a place of the dead below the earth
decisions.reason: παράδεισον is a word borrowed from Persian for a walled park or garden. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8), and in Jewish hope it came to mean the place where God's people are with him. Jesus promises it to the man crucified with him (Luke 23:43), and Revelation 2:7 places the tree of life there.

decisions.choice: unutterable words: things that cannot and may not be spoken
decisions.reason: ἄρρητα can mean "too sacred to be spoken" or "beyond words". The relative clause ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι ("which it is not permitted for a human being to speak") shows the stress falls on what is forbidden: Paul was not allowed to repeat what he heard. So he can boast of the experience but cannot use its content to impress anyone.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "apart from"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read ἐκτὸς, the word used in verse 2, instead of χωρὶς. The meaning is the same. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: things beyond speaking
decisions.reason: "Things" suits English better than "words" here, since what Paul heard is the content of a revelation; "beyond speaking" keeps both sides of the word (m3).

decisions.choice: I also know this about that man ... But I know that ... things too holy to put into words
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the sentence up and says why the words cannot be repeated: they are too holy (m3).

records.source: ὑπὲρ τοῦ τοιούτου καυχήσομαι, ὑπὲρ δὲ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐ καυχήσομαι εἰ μὴ ἐν ταῖς ἀσθενείαις.
records.gloss: On behalf of the such [one] I will boast, on behalf of but myself not I will boast except in the weaknesses.
pieces: About a man like that I will boast, but about myself I will boast only of my weaknesses.

L.5: On behalf of such a [man] I will boast, but on behalf of myself I will not boast, except in [my] weaknesses.

R.5: I will boast about that man. When it comes to myself, the only things I will boast about are my weaknesses.

decisions.choice: boasting about "such a man" but not about "myself": the same person seen two ways
decisions.reason: The man of verses 2-4 is Paul (verse 7), so the contrast is not between two people. Paul will boast of what was given to the man in Christ, because it was God's gift and nothing he did. About himself, as the Corinthians see him, he will boast only of weakness.

decisions.choice: weaknesses: the limits, hardships and humiliations of Paul's life
decisions.reason: ἀσθενείαις covers being weak in every sense: bodily frailty, suffering and lack of standing. The list Paul has just given in 11:23-33, ending with his escape in a basket, shows what he means. These are the things his rivals despise (10:10) and the things through which Christ's power works (12:9).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "the weaknesses", with no "my"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts add "my" after "weaknesses". The sense is the same, since Paul is speaking of his own weaknesses. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: [my] weaknesses (L); my weaknesses (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek article here points to Paul's own weaknesses, which English says with "my".

records.source: ἐὰν γὰρ θελήσω καυχήσασθαι, οὐκ ἔσομαι ἄφρων, ἀλήθειαν γὰρ ἐρῶ· φείδομαι δέ, μή τις εἰς ἐμὲ λογίσηται ὑπὲρ ὃ βλέπει με ἢ ἀκούει τι ἐξ ἐμοῦ, καὶ τῇ ὑπερβολῇ τῶν ἀποκαλύψεων.
records.gloss: If for I should want to boast, not I will be a fool, truth for I will speak; I refrain but, lest anyone to me credit beyond what he sees me or hears anything from me, \v 7 and by the surpassingness of the revelations.
pieces: Should I decide to boast, that would not make me a fool, since it would be the truth I spoke. But I hold back. I do not want anyone to think more of me than what {{gender:they see|he sees}} in me or {{gender:hear|hears}} from me,
or to think more of me because the revelations were so extraordinary.

L.6: For if I should want to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will be speaking [the] truth; but I refrain, so that no one may credit to me more than what {{gender:they see|he sees}} in me or {{gender:hear|hears}} from me,
L.7: even because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations.

R.6: If I chose to boast, I would not really be a fool, because everything I said would be the truth. But I will not do it. I do not want people to think more of me than what they see me do and hear me say.
R.7: And I do not want them to think more of me because the things God showed me were so amazing.

decisions.choice: not a fool, because it would be true: boasting of real revelations would not be folly
decisions.reason: In 11:16-12:10 Paul speaks "as a fool", boasting in the way his rivals do. Here he says that if he chose to boast of experiences like these, he would not really be a fool, because everything he said would be true. The word ἄφρων ("fool") is the same one he uses of his whole speech in 11:16-19 and 12:11.

decisions.choice: I refrain: Paul wants to be judged only by what people can see and hear
alternatives: he is afraid of being disbelieved
decisions.reason: φείδομαι means "I spare, I hold back". λογίσηται is to reckon something to someone's account. Paul does not want anyone to credit him with more than his visible life and his preaching show. Visions cannot be checked, and his rivals evidently built their standing on such claims.

decisions.choice: the phrase about the revelations ends verse 6's sentence, as in the SBLGNT
alternatives: it begins the next sentence: "And because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, therefore, so that I would not become proud, I was given a thorn"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT puts a full stop after καὶ τῇ ὑπερβολῇ τῶν ἀποκαλύψεων ("and by the surpassing greatness of the revelations"), so the phrase finishes verse 6: no one should think more of Paul because of the revelations. Many editions and translations instead begin verse 7 with it: the greatness of the revelations is why the thorn was given. That reading makes the διὸ ("therefore") after it awkward, which is one reason some manuscripts leave that word out (see the next sentence). Either way the revelations are the occasion of the thorn. The evidence is close, so this is uncertain.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they see|he sees}}, {{gender:hear|hears}}
decisions.reason: τις ("anyone") means any person, man or woman, so the pronoun goes through the gender setting. Readable says "people" and needs no setting.

decisions.choice: or to think more of me because the revelations were so extraordinary
alternatives: and by the surpassing greatness of the revelations
decisions.reason: Balanced spells out how the phrase joins the sentence on the SBLGNT reading (m3).

records.source: διὸ ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι, ἐδόθη μοι σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί, ἄγγελος Σατανᾶ, ἵνα με κολαφίζῃ, ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι.
records.gloss: Therefore so that not I may be exalted, was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, so that me he may beat, so that not I may be exalted.
pieces: So, to stop me from becoming too proud, a thorn in the flesh was given to me: a messenger of Satan, sent to beat me down, to stop me from becoming too proud.

L.7: Therefore, so that I would not exalt myself, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan, to beat me, so that I would not exalt myself.

R.7: That is why I was given a painful thorn in my flesh. It was a messenger from Satan, sent to keep hitting me, so that I would not become too proud.

decisions.choice: a thorn in the flesh: some painful, lasting trouble; what it was is not known
decisions.reason: σκόλοψ is a pointed stake or a splinter, here a picture of something that kept piercing Paul. He does not say what it was, and the Corinthians may have known. Proposals include an illness or disability (in Galatians 4:13-15 an illness brought him to Galatia and the Galatians would have given him their eyes; Galatians 6:11 mentions his large letters), his opponents and persecution (in Numbers 33:55 enemies left in the land are "thorns in your sides"), and inner temptation. The last fits poorly with something that humbled him through weakness. The text does not decide, so the rendering keeps Paul's own picture.

decisions.choice: was given: God gave it, though it was a messenger of Satan
decisions.reason: The passive ἐδόθη ("was given") is the way Scripture often speaks of what God does, and the purpose clauses ("so that I would not exalt myself") are God's purpose, not Satan's. As with Job (Job 1-2), Satan means harm, but God uses it for good: here, to keep Paul humble. Satan would hardly aim to stop Paul from being proud.

decisions.choice: a messenger of Satan: an agent sent by Satan
decisions.reason: ἄγγελος means a messenger, human or angelic, and is the usual word for an angel. In apposition to the thorn it names the trouble as Satan's attack. Whether Paul means a personal evil spirit, hostile people, or speaks in a picture cannot be settled, and the rendering "messenger" leaves this open.

decisions.choice: to beat: to strike with the fist, again and again
decisions.reason: κολαφίζῃ is to strike with the fist, as Jesus was struck at his trial (Mark 14:65) and as Paul was treated (1 Corinthians 4:11). The present tense suggests repeated or continuing blows.

decisions.choice: so that I would not exalt myself: to keep Paul from becoming proud
alternatives: so that others would not exalt me
decisions.reason: ὑπεραίρωμαι means to lift oneself up too high, to become arrogant. The clause comes at the beginning and again at the end of the sentence, which stresses the purpose. Some manuscripts do not have the second one.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "therefore" at the start, and the purpose clause twice
decisions.reason: Some important early manuscripts have διὸ ("therefore") and others, with many later manuscripts, leave it out; leaving it out makes it easy to begin the sentence with the end of verse 6 (see the punctuation decision there). Some manuscripts also lack the second ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a thorn in the flesh
decisions.reason: Paul's own picture is kept, because what it stood for is unknown (m1), and "thorn in the flesh" has become an English phrase for a lasting trouble.

decisions.choice: a painful thorn in my flesh
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the picture and adds "painful" and "my" so a young reader sees that it hurt Paul himself, without saying what it was.

decisions.choice: become too proud; beat me down
decisions.reason: Balanced uses plain words for being lifted up in pride and for the repeated blows (m4, m5).

records.source: ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν κύριον παρεκάλεσα ἵνα ἀποστῇ ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ·
records.gloss: Concerning this three times the Lord I begged that it might depart from me;
pieces: I begged the Lord three times about this, asking that it would leave me.

L.8: Concerning this I appealed to the Lord three times, that it might depart from me.

R.8: I asked the Lord three times to make it go away.

decisions.choice: the Lord: Christ
decisions.reason: The answer in verse 9 speaks of "my power" and Paul then calls it "the power of Christ", so the Lord Paul prayed to is the risen Christ. This is one of the places where Paul speaks of praying to Christ.

decisions.choice: appealed: pleaded, earnestly asked
decisions.reason: παρεκάλεσα is the verb that means "comfort" in 1:3-7 and 7:6-7. Here, with an object and a request, it has its other common sense: to call on someone, to plead with him.

decisions.choice: three times: three separate, earnest prayers
decisions.reason: τρὶς most likely means three distinct times of prayer. Jesus also prayed three times in Gethsemane that the cup might pass (Mark 14:32-41), and his request too was answered with something other than removal, but Paul makes no reference to that.

decisions.choice: it: the thorn, also called a messenger of Satan
alternatives: he: the messenger as a person
decisions.reason: τούτου and the subject of ἀποστῇ ("might depart") can be read as "this one" (the messenger) or "this thing" (the thorn). They are the same trouble seen in two ways, so the meaning does not change.

decisions.choice: appealed
decisions.reason: Literal uses a word that fits a prayer (m2); the family is rendered "comfort" only where it means comfort.

records.source: καὶ εἴρηκέν μοι· Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου· ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται.
records.gloss: And he has said to me, "Suffices for you the grace of me; the for power in weakness is brought to completion."
pieces: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} answered me, "My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness."

L.9: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has said to me, "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is brought to completion in weakness."

R.9: But the Lord answered me, "My grace is enough for you. Power does its greatest work where there is weakness."

decisions.choice: has said: an answer given once that still stands
decisions.reason: εἴρηκέν is in the perfect tense: the Lord gave his answer, and it remains his word to Paul. The thorn was not taken away; the answer replaced the request.

decisions.choice: my grace is enough: the Lord's favor and help are all Paul needs
alternatives: grace as an inner strength apart from Christ
decisions.reason: Ἀρκεῖ means "is enough, is sufficient". χάρις is the Lord's undeserved favor, which in Paul includes his active help (1 Corinthians 15:10: "by the grace of God I am what I am"). The speaker is Christ (verse 8), so it is Christ's grace.

decisions.choice: power is brought to completion in weakness: power does its full work where human strength fails
decisions.reason: τελεῖται means to complete, to carry through to its goal. The power is the Lord's (verse 9b names it "the power of Christ"). It reaches its full effect in weakness, where nothing human can take the credit, as the clay pots of 4:7 show.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "power", with no "my"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "my" ("my power"), the reading of the King James Version. The SBLGNT text has none. The sense is little affected, since the next sentence calls it the power of Christ. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers to the Lord Christ. "My" at the start of his words is capitalized in any case and needs no setting; Readable says "the Lord".

decisions.choice: grace
decisions.reason: Grace is a key term and keeps its word at every level.

decisions.choice: is enough; comes to its fullness (B); does its greatest work (R)
decisions.reason: "Made perfect" can suggest moral perfection; Balanced and Readable say that power reaches its full effect (m3).

decisions.choice: the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker, the Lord of verse 8.

records.source: ἥδιστα οὖν μᾶλλον καυχήσομαι ἐν ταῖς ἀσθενείαις μου, ἵνα ἐπισκηνώσῃ ἐπ’ ἐμὲ ἡ δύναμις τοῦ Χριστοῦ.
records.gloss: Most gladly therefore rather I will boast in the weaknesses of me, so that may tent upon me the power of the Christ.
pieces: So I will be all the happier to boast of my weaknesses, for then the power of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} may spread its tent over me.

L.9: Most gladly, therefore, I will rather boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} may pitch [its] tent over me.

R.9: So I am very glad to boast about my weaknesses. Then the power of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will stay over me like a tent.

decisions.choice: most gladly, rather: instead of asking for the weakness to go, Paul will boast of it
decisions.reason: ἥδιστα is "most gladly". μᾶλλον ("rather") sets this against his prayer in verse 8: instead of begging to be rid of weakness, he will boast of it. It may also mean "all the more"; the point is the same.

decisions.choice: may pitch its tent over me: may come to dwell on me and shelter me
decisions.reason: ἐπισκηνώσῃ is built on the word for a tent and means to take up lodging, to dwell. The picture is of Christ's power settling over Paul as a dwelling and a shelter.

decisions.choice: the tent may recall God dwelling with his people
decisions.reason: The tent word family is used of God's dwelling among Israel in the tabernacle, where his glory filled the tent (Exodus 40:34-35), and of the Word who "tented" among us (John 1:14). Paul may hint that Christ's power dwells with him as God's presence dwelt in the tent. The verb itself does not prove this.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting, as everywhere.

decisions.choice: pitch [its] tent over (L); spread its tent over (B); stay over me like a tent (R)
decisions.reason: Each level keeps the tent in the verb (m2), which "rest upon" loses.

decisions.choice: boast
decisions.reason: As in 12:1, "boast" is kept at every level in these chapters.

records.source: διὸ εὐδοκῶ ἐν ἀσθενείαις, ἐν ὕβρεσιν, ἐν ἀνάγκαις, ἐν διωγμοῖς καὶ στενοχωρίαις, ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ· ὅταν γὰρ ἀσθενῶ, τότε δυνατός εἰμι.
records.gloss: Therefore I am well pleased in weaknesses, in insults, in calamities, in persecutions and tight places, for the sake of Christ; whenever for I am weak, then strong I am.
pieces: That is why I am glad to have weaknesses, insults, calamities, persecutions and tight corners, for the sake of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. For it is when I am weak that I am strong.

L.10: Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults, in calamities, in persecutions and tight places, for the sake of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}; for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.

R.10: So for {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}'s sake I am glad when I am weak, when people insult me, when disasters come, when I am persecuted, and when I feel trapped. For when I am weak, that is when I am strong.

decisions.choice: I take pleasure in: I gladly accept, I am content with
alternatives: I enjoy suffering for its own sake
decisions.reason: εὐδοκῶ is to be well pleased with something, to approve it gladly. Paul does not enjoy pain; he welcomes these things because, endured for Christ's sake, they are where Christ's power is at work (verse 9).

decisions.choice: for the sake of Christ: applies to the whole list
decisions.reason: ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ comes at the end and covers every item. These are hardships suffered because Paul serves Christ, not every misfortune.

decisions.choice: insults, calamities, persecutions, tight places
decisions.reason: ὕβρεσιν is insulting, humiliating treatment. ἀνάγκαις is distress or calamity, and στενοχωρίαις is being hemmed in with no way out; both stand in the list of 6:4. διωγμοῖς is persecution for the faith.

decisions.choice: when I am weak, then I am strong: Christ's strength, not Paul's
alternatives: weakness itself is a kind of strength
decisions.reason: The strength is the power of Christ that dwells on Paul (verse 9). His weakness is the place where that power is seen, so the paradox sums up verses 7-10.

decisions.choice: calamities, tight places (L); calamities, tight corners (B); disasters, feel trapped (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as in the list of 6:4, so the two lists can be compared; "hardship" is kept for the word rendered "affliction" at Literal (1:4; 4:17).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

records.source: Γέγονα ἄφρων· ὑμεῖς με ἠναγκάσατε· ἐγὼ γὰρ ὤφειλον ὑφ’ ὑμῶν συνίστασθαι.
records.gloss: I have become a fool; you me compelled; I for ought by you to be commended.
pieces: I have become a fool. You forced me into it. It was you who should have been recommending me.

L.11: I have become a fool; you forced me. For I ought to have been commended by you.

R.11: I have been acting like a fool. But you made me do it. You should have been the ones recommending me.

decisions.choice: I have become a fool: Paul looks back on his fool's speech
alternatives: Paul admits he is truly foolish
decisions.reason: Γέγονα is perfect: the boasting of 11:16-12:10 is done and stands as said. Paul took on the role of a fool (11:16-17, 21) to answer rivals on their own terms. The word ἄφρων is the same as in 11:16 and 12:6.

decisions.choice: you, emphatic: the Corinthians are to blame
decisions.reason: Both ὑμεῖς ("you") and ἐγὼ ("I") are emphatic. The Corinthians forced him by failing to defend him against the rivals. The imperfect ὤφειλον ("I ought") states what should have happened and did not.

decisions.choice: commended: spoken for, recommended
decisions.reason: συνίστασθαι is the verb of recommendation that runs through the letter (3:1; 4:2; 5:12; 10:12, 18). The Corinthians, who owed their faith to Paul, should have been his letter of recommendation (3:2).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "I have become a fool", with no added word
alternatives: "I have become a fool in boasting"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add a participle meaning "boasting" after "fool", which is the reading of the King James Version. The SBLGNT text does not have it. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a fool (L, B); acting like a fool (R)
decisions.reason: "Fool" keeps the link with the fool's speech of chapter 11 (11:16-19); Readable says that Paul played the part.

decisions.choice: recommending
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "recommend" for this verb, as in 4:2 and chapter 10.

records.heading: Paul's concern for the Corinthians

records.source: οὐδὲν γὰρ ὑστέρησα τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων, εἰ καὶ οὐδέν εἰμι·
records.gloss: Nothing for I lacked [compared to] the super-extra apostles, if even nothing I am;
pieces: In nothing did I fall short of these super-apostles, even if I am nothing.

L.11: For in nothing did I fall short of the super-apostles, even if I am nothing.

R.11: Those so-called super-apostles are not one bit better than I am, even though I am nothing.

decisions.choice: the super-apostles: Paul's mocking name for his rivals in Corinth
decisions.reason: ὑπερλίαν means "beyond measure, exceedingly". Paul used the same phrase in 11:5. The phrase mocks people who rate themselves very highly. Most likely they are the rivals of 10:12 and 11:12-15, whom Paul calls false apostles; some think they are the leading apostles in Jerusalem, whose names the rivals invoked. In 11:13 Paul speaks of the rivals in much harsher terms, which some take as a sign that two groups are meant.

decisions.choice: I did not fall short: during his time among them
decisions.reason: ὑστέρησα is aorist and looks back to Paul's ministry in Corinth, which verse 12 goes on to describe.

decisions.choice: even if I am nothing: real humility, with an edge
decisions.reason: εἰ καὶ οὐδέν εἰμι means "even though I am nothing". In himself Paul claims nothing (1 Corinthians 3:7; 15:9-10), and what he is he owes to grace. At the same time the phrase turns the rivals' scorn back on them: if he is nothing, they are less.

decisions.choice: super-apostles (L, B); those so-called super-apostles (R)
decisions.reason: "Super-apostles" keeps the mocking tone of the phrase (m1). Readable adds "so-called" so a young reader sees that Paul is using their own high opinion of themselves, in the same words as 11:5.

records.source: τὰ μὲν σημεῖα τοῦ ἀποστόλου κατειργάσθη ἐν ὑμῖν ἐν πάσῃ ὑπομονῇ, σημείοις τε καὶ τέρασιν καὶ δυνάμεσιν.
records.gloss: The indeed signs of the apostle were worked among you in all endurance, by signs both and wonders and powerful deeds.
pieces: Among you, with all endurance, the signs that mark an apostle were done: signs, wonders and deeds of power.

L.12: The signs of the apostle were indeed performed among you in all endurance, by signs and wonders and powerful deeds.

R.12: The signs that prove someone is an apostle were done among you. I kept going patiently through everything, and there were signs, wonders and miracles.

decisions.choice: the signs of the apostle: the marks that show a true apostle
decisions.reason: The article in τοῦ ἀποστόλου is generic: "the apostle" is any true apostle. The first σημεῖα are the evidences of apostleship; the end of the sentence names the miracles among them.

decisions.choice: were performed: done among them, by God through Paul
alternatives: Paul performed them by his own power
decisions.reason: The passive κατειργάσθη lets Paul avoid saying "I did". In Romans 15:18-19 he speaks of what Christ worked through him "by the power of signs and wonders".

decisions.choice: indeed: the sentence implies "but you did not take notice"
decisions.reason: μὲν usually looks ahead to a contrasting "but". None follows, and the unspoken contrast is the Corinthians' failure to recognize what they had seen, which leads into verse 13.

decisions.choice: endurance: perseverance under hardship
decisions.reason: ὑπομονῇ is the endurance of 1:6 and 6:4. The signs were done in the middle of hardship, which fits the weakness Paul has just boasted of.

decisions.choice: signs, wonders and deeds of power: three words for miracles
decisions.reason: The three words often go together (Acts 2:22; Romans 15:19). A sign points beyond itself, a wonder astonishes, and a deed of power shows God's might; the same events can be all three.

decisions.choice: signs
decisions.reason: Sign is a key term and is kept for both uses, even where the first means "evidences" (m1).

decisions.choice: powerful deeds (L); deeds of power (B); miracles (R)
decisions.reason: δυνάμεσιν is the plural of the word for power, here acts of power; Readable uses the everyday word.

decisions.choice: I kept going patiently through everything
decisions.reason: Readable says whose endurance is meant: Paul's, during his time among them.

records.source: τί γάρ ἐστιν ὃ ἡσσώθητε ὑπὲρ τὰς λοιπὰς ἐκκλησίας, εἰ μὴ ὅτι αὐτὸς ἐγὼ οὐ κατενάρκησα ὑμῶν;
records.gloss: What for is it which you were made inferior beyond the rest churches, except that myself I not burdened you?
pieces: In what way were you put at a disadvantage compared with the other churches, except that I myself never lived off you?

L.13: For in what were you treated worse than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you?

R.13: The only way I treated you worse than the other churches was this: I did not ask you to support me.

decisions.choice: burden: be a financial burden, live at their expense
decisions.reason: κατενάρκησα is to weigh on someone, here by taking support. Paul used the same verb in 11:9: in Corinth he took nothing from them and was supported by believers from Macedonia (compare 1 Corinthians 9:12-18).

decisions.choice: you were treated worse: made to come off worse than other churches
decisions.reason: ἡσσώθητε means to be made inferior, to lose out. The rivals seem to have argued that Paul's refusal of support showed he did not love the Corinthians, or that he was no real apostle (11:7-11).

decisions.choice: an ironic question
decisions.reason: The question answers itself: the only "disadvantage" the Corinthians suffered was that Paul cost them nothing.

decisions.choice: lived off you (B); ask you to support me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of burden Paul means (m1).

records.source: χαρίσασθέ μοι τὴν ἀδικίαν ταύτην.
records.gloss: Forgive me the wrong this.
pieces: Please forgive me for this injustice!

R.13: Please forgive me for being so unfair to you!

decisions.choice: forgive me this wrong: biting irony
decisions.reason: Paul calls his refusal of their money a ἀδικίαν ("wrong, injustice") only in irony: the "wrong" was that he served them for free.

decisions.choice: forgive: pardon as a favor
decisions.reason: χαρίσασθέ comes from the same root as grace and means to give freely, here to forgive, as in 2:7, 10.

decisions.choice: an exclamation mark
decisions.reason: The exclamation lets the irony be heard (m1).

records.source: Ἰδοὺ τρίτον τοῦτο ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς, καὶ οὐ καταναρκήσω· οὐ γὰρ ζητῶ τὰ ὑμῶν ἀλλὰ ὑμᾶς, οὐ γὰρ ὀφείλει τὰ τέκνα τοῖς γονεῦσιν θησαυρίζειν, ἀλλὰ οἱ γονεῖς τοῖς τέκνοις.
records.gloss: Look, third [time] this I am ready to come to you, and not I will be a burden; not for I seek the [things] of you but you, not for ought the children for the parents to store up, but the parents for the children.
pieces: Here I am, ready to come to you for the third time, and I will not live off you. I am not after your money; I am after you. It is not for children to put money aside for their parents; it is parents who put it aside for their children.

L.14: Look, this [is the] third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden; for I do not seek what is yours but you; for the children ought not to store up for the parents, but the parents for the children.

R.14: This will be the third time I visit you, and I am ready to come. I will not ask you to support me. I do not want your money. I want you. It is not the children's job to save money for their parents. Parents save money for their children.

decisions.choice: the third time: Paul's third visit to Corinth
alternatives: the third time he has got ready, without coming
decisions.reason: τρίτον τοῦτο could mean that this is the third time Paul has been ready to come. But 13:1 says plainly "this is the third time I am coming to you", so a third visit is meant: the first when he founded the church (Acts 18), the second the painful visit (2:1), and now a third.

decisions.choice: not what is yours but you: not their money but themselves
alternatives: not their praise but their obedience
decisions.reason: τὰ ὑμῶν ("the things of you") are their possessions. Paul wants the Corinthians themselves, their faith and love, as 12:15 goes on to say.

decisions.choice: parents save up for their children: Paul speaks as their father
alternatives: a general rule about inheritance law
decisions.reason: It was the normal duty of parents to provide for their children, not the other way round. Paul calls himself the Corinthians' father in the faith (1 Corinthians 4:14-15; 2 Corinthians 6:13), so he will not take from them.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "I will not be a burden", with no "to you"
alternatives: "I will not be a burden to you"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts add "to you". The meaning is the same. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: live off you; your money (B); ask you to support me; your money (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say outright that the burden and the possessions are money (m2), as in verse 13.

records.heading: Ready to come a third time

records.source: ἐγὼ δὲ ἥδιστα δαπανήσω καὶ ἐκδαπανηθήσομαι ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: I but most gladly will spend and will be spent out on behalf of the souls of you.
pieces: For my part, I will gladly spend everything I have, and spend myself to the last, for your sake.

L.15: And I will most gladly spend and be utterly spent for your souls.

R.15: I am very happy to spend everything I have for you, and even to use up my whole life for you.

decisions.choice: spend and be utterly spent: give his means and himself
decisions.reason: δαπανήσω is to spend money or resources; ἐκδαπανηθήσομαι is the passive of a stronger form, to be used up completely. The step from the one to the other moves from what Paul has to what he is.

decisions.choice: your souls: you yourselves, your lives
alternatives: the soul as opposed to the body
decisions.reason: ψυχῶν here means the whole person and life, as often in Paul (1 Thessalonians 2:8). Paul spends himself for their good as persons.

decisions.choice: for your sake (B); for you (R)
decisions.reason: "Souls" in English can suggest the inner part only; Balanced and Readable say "for you" (m2).

records.source: εἰ περισσοτέρως ὑμᾶς ἀγαπῶν, ἧσσον ἀγαπῶμαι;
records.gloss: If more abundantly you loving, less am I loved?
pieces: If I love you so much more, does that mean you love me less?

L.15: If, loving you all the more, I am loved less?

R.15: I love you more and more. Should that make you love me less?

decisions.choice: a question: should more love from Paul mean less love from them?
alternatives: a statement: though I love you more, I am loved less
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates the sentence as a question, which makes it a rebuke. Read as a statement it is a lament. Either way Paul's love is met with less love in return, so the meaning is close.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "if" with the participle "loving"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "even if" and a finite verb, "even if I love you more". The meaning is the same. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

records.source: ἔστω δέ, ἐγὼ οὐ κατεβάρησα ὑμᾶς· ἀλλὰ ὑπάρχων πανοῦργος δόλῳ ὑμᾶς ἔλαβον.
records.gloss: Let it be but, I not burdened you; but being crafty by deceit you I took.
pieces: Granted, I myself did not weigh you down. Still, some say I was cunning and caught you with a trick.

L.16: But let it be so: I did not burden you. "But, being crafty, I took you by deceit."

R.16: Some of you agree that I did not make you pay for me. But they say I was sly and tricked you.

decisions.choice: the second half voices a charge made against Paul
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has no quotation marks, but ἀλλὰ ὑπάρχων πανοῦργος δόλῳ ὑμᾶς ἔλαβον ("but being crafty, I took you by deceit") is not something Paul admits. He repeats what some were saying, in his own voice and with irony: that he took no support openly but got their money in a cunning way. Verses 17-18 answer exactly that charge. Who made it, the rivals or some in the church, is not said.

decisions.choice: crafty, by deceit: cunning trickery for gain
decisions.reason: πανοῦργος is a cunning, unscrupulous person, and δόλῳ is deceit or a trap; ὑμᾶς ἔλαβον is to catch someone, like prey. The charge seems to be that the collection for Jerusalem (chapters 8-9) was a way to get money from them through others (verses 17-18).

decisions.choice: let it be so: granted
decisions.reason: ἔστω δέ grants a point for argument: "all right, granted". It is the Corinthians' admission that Paul himself took nothing.

decisions.choice: quotation marks
decisions.reason: Literal marks the charge with quotation marks, as other quoted sayings in these letters are marked (m1).

decisions.choice: some say (B); Some of you agree ... But they say (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say outright that this is what others claim (m1). Readable also makes the admission in the first half theirs (m3).

decisions.choice: weigh you down
decisions.reason: This verb differs from the one in verses 13-14, so Balanced uses a different phrase for it.

records.source: μή τινα ὧν ἀπέσταλκα πρὸς ὑμᾶς, δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐπλεονέκτησα ὑμᾶς;
records.gloss: Not anyone of whom I have sent to you, through him did I take advantage of you?
pieces: Take any one of those I have sent to you: did I use any of them to cheat you?

L.17: Any of those whom I have sent to you, did I exploit you through him?

R.17: I sent some people to you. Did I use any of them to cheat you? No!

decisions.choice: a question expecting "no", with a broken construction
decisions.reason: μή marks a question that expects the answer "no". The sentence starts with "any of those I have sent" and then restarts with "through him".

decisions.choice: exploit: take advantage of someone for gain
decisions.reason: ἐπλεονέκτησα is to take more than one's share, to cheat for gain. Paul uses it in 7:2, where he says he has cheated no one.

decisions.choice: exploit (L); cheat (B, R)
decisions.reason: The same words as in 7:2.

decisions.choice: No!
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the Greek question expects (m1).

records.source: παρεκάλεσα Τίτον καὶ συναπέστειλα τὸν ἀδελφόν· μήτι ἐπλεονέκτησεν ὑμᾶς Τίτος;
records.gloss: I urged Titus and I sent with [him] the brother; not did take advantage of you Titus?
pieces: I urged Titus to go, and I sent the brother with him. Titus did not cheat you, did he?

L.18: I urged Titus [to go], and I sent the brother with [him]. Titus did not exploit you, did he?

R.18: I asked Titus to visit you, and I sent the other brother with him. Titus did not cheat you, did he?

decisions.choice: an earlier visit by Titus, with a brother
decisions.reason: The verbs are aorist and Paul appeals to how Titus behaved, so the visit had already happened. It is most likely the visit when Titus began the collection (8:6). Some read it as the sending described in 8:16-24, written from the readers' point of view, but there Titus goes with two brothers, not one.

decisions.choice: the brother: a believer the Corinthians knew, one particular man
decisions.reason: τὸν ἀδελφόν is a fellow believer, known to the readers and not named here. He is one particular man.

decisions.choice: a question expecting "no"
decisions.reason: μήτι marks a question that expects the answer "no".

decisions.choice: the brother, with no gender setting
decisions.reason: He is one particular man (m2), so no gender setting applies, as in 8:18.

decisions.choice: Titus did not ..., did he?
decisions.reason: A tag question shows that the expected answer is "no" (m3).

records.source: οὐ τῷ αὐτῷ πνεύματι περιεπατήσαμεν;
records.gloss: Not in the same spirit did we walk?
pieces: Did we not conduct ourselves in the same spirit?

L.18: Did we not walk in the same spirit?

R.18: He and I always acted in the same way, did we not?

decisions.choice: the same spirit: the same attitude and way of acting
decisions.reason: τῷ αὐτῷ πνεύματι may mean the Holy Spirit, who led Paul and Titus alike, or the same spirit in the sense of attitude. The parallel question "in the same footsteps?" points to the manner of their conduct, so a small letter is used; but Paul often speaks of walking by the Spirit (Galatians 5:16, 25), and both may be in view.

decisions.choice: walk: live, conduct oneself
decisions.reason: περιεπατήσαμεν ("we walked") is Paul's usual picture for a way of life.

decisions.choice: we: Paul and Titus
decisions.reason: The "we" here joins Paul with Titus.

decisions.choice: spirit, with a small letter
decisions.reason: A small letter follows the reading in m1, which is uncertain.

records.source: οὐ τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἴχνεσιν;
records.gloss: Not in the same footsteps?
pieces: Did we not tread in the same footsteps?

R.18: We did things the same way, did we not?

decisions.choice: the same footsteps: following the same path
decisions.reason: ἴχνεσιν are footprints. To walk in the same footsteps is to follow the same path, here the same honest conduct.

decisions.choice: Did we not tread
decisions.reason: Balanced supplies the verb from the question before.

records.source: Πάλαι δοκεῖτε ὅτι ὑμῖν ἀπολογούμεθα;
records.gloss: All along you think that to you we are making a defense?
pieces: Have you supposed this whole time that we are pleading our case before you?

L.19: All along you have been thinking that we are making our defense to you?

R.19: Do you think that all this time we have been trying to prove our innocence to you?

decisions.choice: making a defense: pleading one's case before judges
decisions.reason: ἀπολογούμεθα is the word for a defense in court. Paul does not accept the Corinthians as his judges; the next sentence names his real judge.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "all along"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read a similar word meaning "again" instead of Πάλαι ("for a long time, all along"), the reading of the King James Version. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a question, as in the SBLGNT
alternatives: a statement: you have been thinking all along that we are defending ourselves
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT prints a question mark. As a statement the sentence would say what they think and then correct it; as a question it challenges them. The meaning is close either way.

decisions.choice: we: Paul himself, perhaps with his coworkers
decisions.reason: As through much of the letter (see 1:8), "we" is mostly Paul himself.

records.source: κατέναντι θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ λαλοῦμεν.
records.gloss: Before God in Christ we speak.
pieces: We are speaking in the sight of God, as those who are in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

R.19: God is watching as we speak, and we speak as people who belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: before God, in Christ: God is the judge Paul answers to
decisions.reason: The same words appear in 2:17. Paul speaks answerable to God and as one united with Christ, not as a defendant before the Corinthians.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

records.source: τὰ δὲ πάντα, ἀγαπητοί, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν οἰκοδομῆς, φοβοῦμαι γὰρ μή πως ἐλθὼν οὐχ οἵους θέλω εὕρω ὑμᾶς, κἀγὼ εὑρεθῶ ὑμῖν οἷον οὐ θέλετε, μή πως ἔρις, ζῆλος, θυμοί, ἐριθεῖαι, καταλαλιαί, ψιθυρισμοί, φυσιώσεις, ἀκαταστασίαι·
records.gloss: The but all things, beloved, [are] for the of you building up. \v 20 I fear for lest perhaps having come not such as I want I may find you, and I may be found by you such as not you want; lest perhaps strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish ambitions, slanders, whisperings, puffings up, disorders;
pieces: Everything we do, dear friends, is to build you up.

For I fear that I may come and find you other than I wish, and that you may find me other than you wish. I fear there may be quarreling, jealousy, outbursts of anger, rivalry, slander, whispering behind backs, people puffed up with pride, and disorder.

L.19: And all things, beloved, [are] for your building up.
L.20: For I fear that perhaps, having come, I may find you not such as I want, and I may be found by you such as you do not want; that perhaps [there may be] strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish ambitions, slanders, whisperings, puffings up, disorders.

R.19: Everything we do, dear friends, is to build you up.
R.20: I worry that when I arrive, I will find you living in ways I do not like, and you will find me acting in ways you will not like. I am afraid that you will be quarreling, jealous, and losing your tempers. I am afraid some of you will be trying to get ahead of others, saying bad things about each other, gossiping, being proud, and causing disorder.

decisions.choice: all for your building up: everything Paul says and does aims at their growth
decisions.reason: οἰκοδομῆς is building up, the purpose for which the Lord gave Paul his authority (10:8; 13:10). Even the boasting and the defense are for the Corinthians' good. ἀγαπητοί ("beloved") shows his affection even as he warns.

decisions.choice: you may find me as you do not wish: Paul may have to act with severity
decisions.reason: If he finds them unchanged, he will come with discipline, not gentleness (1 Corinthians 4:21; 2 Corinthians 13:2, 10). That is the side of him they do not want to see.

decisions.choice: the list: sins that tear a church apart
alternatives: sins of the pagan world only
decisions.reason: ἔρις ζῆλος ("strife, jealousy") are the words of 1 Corinthians 3:3, where they show the divisions. θυμοί are outbursts of anger. ἐριθεῖαι is selfish ambition and rivalry (Philippians 2:3). καταλαλιαί is speaking against others and ψιθυρισμοί whispered gossip. φυσιώσεις is being "puffed up", the Corinthians' pride (1 Corinthians 4:6, 18; 8:1). ἀκαταστασίαι here is disorder in the church, as in 1 Corinthians 14:33, not riots in the streets as in 6:5.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "strife, jealousy" in the singular
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have these first two words in the plural, like the rest of the list. The meaning is the same. The SBLGNT text is followed. Reviewers must check the manuscript evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: we: Paul himself
decisions.reason: The "we" of verse 19 is Paul (with his coworkers), and he goes on in the first person singular in verse 20.

decisions.choice: strife, jealousy, selfish ambitions, puffings up (L); quarreling, jealousy, rivalry, puffed up with pride (B); quarreling, jealous, trying to get ahead, proud (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as in 1 Corinthians 3:3 and Philippians 2:3, and "puffed up" (Readable "proud") as in 1 Corinthians 4 and 8.

decisions.choice: I fear there may be (B); I am afraid that ... (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat the verb of fearing so that the list can stand as a sentence.

decisions.choice: beloved (L); dear friends (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 7:1.

records.source: μὴ πάλιν ἐλθόντος μου ταπεινώσῃ με ὁ θεός μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς, καὶ πενθήσω πολλοὺς τῶν προημαρτηκότων καὶ μὴ μετανοησάντων ἐπὶ τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ καὶ πορνείᾳ καὶ ἀσελγείᾳ ᾗ ἔπραξαν.
records.gloss: Lest again having come me may humble me the God of me before you, and I may mourn many of those having sinned before and not having repented of the impurity and sexual immorality and sensuality which they practiced.
pieces: I fear that when I come, my God may again bring me low in front of you, and that I may have to mourn over many who sinned in the past and still have not repented of what they did: impurity, sexual immorality and indecency.

L.21: [I fear] that again, when I come, my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who have sinned before and have not repented of the impurity and sexual immorality and sensuality that they practiced.

R.21: I am afraid that on my visit my God will make me feel low and ashamed in front of you again. I am afraid I will cry over many people who sinned before and have not turned away from what was wrong. They have done impure things, sexual sins and shameless things.

decisions.choice: the fear goes on from verse 20
alternatives: a new sentence with no link
decisions.reason: μὴ repeats the "lest" of verse 20, so this is a further thing Paul fears.

decisions.choice: "again" goes with being humbled: Paul fears a second humbling visit
decisions.reason: πάλιν stands between the start of the sentence and "when I come". It can go with the coming ("when I come again") or with the humbling ("may humble me again"). Since Paul's last visit was a painful one (2:1), many read it as a fear of being humbled again.

decisions.choice: humble: bring low, put to shame
decisions.reason: ταπεινώσῃ here is to bring someone low. A father is shamed by his children's conduct; Paul would be humiliated before them if his converts were still living in sin. He says God may allow this.

decisions.choice: mourn over those who sinned and did not repent
decisions.reason: πενθήσω is to mourn, as for the dead (compare 1 Corinthians 5:2). προημαρτηκότων is perfect: they sinned before, perhaps before the painful visit, and the sin continues. They have not repented. Paul's mourning may include the discipline he will have to carry out (13:2).

decisions.choice: impurity, sexual immorality, sensuality
decisions.reason: ἀκαθαρσίᾳ is moral impurity, πορνείᾳ sexual immorality of every kind (1 Corinthians 5:1; 6:18), and ἀσελγείᾳ unrestrained, shameless indecency. The same words appear together in Galatians 5:19.

decisions.choice: impurity, sexual immorality, sensuality (L); impurity, sexual immorality, indecency (B); impure things, sexual sins, shameless things (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as in Colossians 3:5 and Ephesians 4:19, where these terms appear.

decisions.choice: turned away from what was wrong
decisions.reason: Readable explains repentance in plain words, as the book-wide choice for this word family does.

decisions.choice: [I fear]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the verb of fearing from verse 20 (m1).
